messages.subject: [statnet_help] anyone know how to extract largest connected subnetwork from a netowrk object
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] anyone know how to extract largest connected subnetwork from a netowrk object
messages.body_plain:
I don't know if this was ever satisfactorily answered, but the general
method I use to extract a subnetwork is to create a copy of the source
network using network.copy()*, then delete from the copy the nodes I don't
want. This retains all the attribute data for the sub-network. (*If you use
regular assignment to create a copy of your network then any vertices
deleted from the child network object will also be deleted from the parent
network object for some reason!)

I've included two example functions (below my sig). The firstextracts the
largest component from a network; the second extracts a network consisting
of all nodes sharing a specified vertex attribute value. I think these
functions should be pretty generic, though I've only tested them on two
networks.

Cheers,
Dave
____________________________
David A. Nolin
Postdoctoral Scholar
Carolina Population Center
University of North Carolina


### Function to extract largest component of a network:
### Step 1: Create network copy of source network
### Step 2: Extract node set of largest component
### Step 3: Define a cut set consisting of all other nodes
### Step 4: Delete nodes not in largest component from network copy

extract.lc.net<-function(x){
temp<-network.copy(x)
temp.lc<-component.largest(temp)
cut.set<-row(as.matrix(temp.lc))[temp.lc==F]
temp<-delete.vertices(temp, cut.set)
return(temp)}

### Load example data
data("faux.magnolia.high")

### Extract largest component
fmh.lc<-extract.lc.net(faux.magnolia.high)

### Test: check that new network is same size as largest component
network.size(fmh.lc)
length(component.largest(faux.magnolia.high)[component.largest(faux.magnolia.high)==T])

### Check that attributes are attached
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.lc)


### Function to extract a network of all nodes having a specified attribute
value
extract.att.net<-function(net,att,val){
temp<-network.copy(net)
nodes.having.val<-temp%v%att==val
cut.set<-row(as.matrix(nodes.having.val))[nodes.having.val==F]
temp<-delete.vertices(temp, cut.set)
return(temp)}

### Test: extract seperate networks of all females and males from
faux.magnolia.high
fmh.F<-extract.att.net(faux.magnolia.high, "Sex", "F")
fmh.M<-extract.att.net(faux.magnolia.high, "Sex", "M")

### Check result
network.size(fmh.F)
network.size(fmh.M)
table(faux.magnolia.high%v%"Sex")

### Check that attributes are attached:
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.F)
list.vertex.attributes(fmh.M)

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about measuring associations among a set of valued networks
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I've got 9 valued networks each one with 24 actors and each one for 8
different countries., i.e., totally 72 valued graphs, and I would like
to compute the QAP correlation among all pairs of networks in this set
(i.e., 2,556 pairs of networks).

I was wondering if there is an automatic way to obtain this
correlation matrix altogether instead of running it separately for
each pair of networks.

Also: what is the QAP command in statnet? If I knew this, I might try
to program the total computation in R.

Best,

--Moses

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Question about measuring associations among a set of	valued networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Question about measuring associations among a set of	valued networks
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Moses.  To get graph correlations/covariances, try gcor and gcov. 
(gscor and gscov do the same thing for partially labeled structures; see 
also hdist and structdist for distances.)  If passed multiple graphs, 
these will return the appropriate correlation/covariance matrix (and the 
data can be valued).  QAP is a permutation procedure that provides a 
null distribution for bivariate graph statistics (e.g., the graph 
correlation, Hubert's gamma, Hamming distance, etc.), so there's not 
actually such a thing as a "QAP Correlation" per se.  The correlations 
and such obtained from the above can, however, be compared against QAP 
nulls using the qaptest command.  For a related parametric approach, try 
the optional netperm package.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] decay for gwidegree
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I'm not a big user of the directed gw* terms, but for the undirected ones 
my general rule of thumb is to start low with the decay term.  As a 
general rule of thumb for empirical data, the lower the decay term is, the 
less likely the model is to be degenerate. So I typically start around 
0.25 or so.  For data I've worked with I often find there is little 
diffence in model fit across a range of decay terms, often 0.5 to 1.5 or 
so. But then again, I've only applied these to a specific social network 
domain (adolescent friendship nets) and the details of my experience may 
not be universal.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Modelling 'combined' homophily
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
This may be a newbie question, so apologies in advance. 
I am trying to run a model for a dataset of fund managers and brokers. It is an undirected network of 26 nodes and 70 ties. Each node has two attributes: ?type?, which can get one of two categorical values (either ?fund manager? or ?broker) and ?last job?, which can get one of 11 values. The effect I would like to model is the following: if, for two nodes, the ?type? value is identical and equals ?fund manager? and, for the same two nodes, ?last job? is identical then I expect to find homophily above chance. In contrast, if the two nodes? ?type? variable is different  or both nodes have ?broker? as ?type? then I would not expect to find significant homophily.
I am not sure how to model. In case this helps, I used the following model to check for the ?non-combined? effect (?type? on its own and ?last job? on its own):

> m2.7<-ergm( g ~ edges + nodematch("type") + nodematch("lastjob") )
> summary(m2.7)

==========================
Summary of model fit
==========================

Formula:   g ~ edges + nodematch("type") + nodematch("lastjob")

Newton-Raphson iterations:  5 

Maximum Likelihood Results:
                  Estimate Std. Error MCMC s.e.  p-value    
edges              -0.3711     0.2024        NA 0.067721 .  
nodematch.type     -2.0826     0.3176        NA  < 1e-04 ***
nodematch.lastjob   1.5025     0.4079        NA 0.000269 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ?***? 0.001 ?**? 0.01 ?*? 0.05 ?.? 0.1 ? ? 1 

For this model, the pseudolikelihood is the same as the likelihood.

    Null  Deviance: 450.55  on 325  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 282.39  on 322  degrees of freedom
          Deviance: 168.16  on   3  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 288.39    BIC: 299.74

I also tried to combine the ?type? and ?last job? to one variable, but then the results were not significant:

> m2.71<-ergm( g ~ edges + nodematch("type") + nodematch("lastjob") + nodematch("typelastjob") )
> summary(m2.71)

==========================
Summary of model fit
==========================

Formula:   g ~ edges + nodematch("type") + nodematch("lastjob") + nodematch("typelastjob")

Newton-Raphson iterations:  6 

Maximum Likelihood Results:
                      Estimate Std. Error MCMC s.e. p-value    
edges                  -0.3365     0.2070        NA   0.105    
nodematch.type         -2.1778     0.3465        NA  <1e-04 ***
nodematch.lastjob       1.0296     0.7368        NA   0.163    
nodematch.typelastjob   0.6517     0.8738        NA   0.456    
---
Signif. codes:  0 ?***? 0.001 ?**? 0.01 ?*? 0.05 ?.? 0.1 ? ? 1 

For this model, the pseudolikelihood is the same as the likelihood.

    Null  Deviance: 450.55  on 325  degrees of freedom
 Residual Deviance: 281.85  on 321  degrees of freedom
          Deviance: 168.70  on   4  degrees of freedom
 
AIC: 289.85    BIC: 304.98

So, any ideas how I can go about modelling this effect would be highly appreciated.
Many thanks,
Yuval

messages.body_plain:
Hi Yuval,

One thing you can try it to use nodematch("type", diff = TRUE) instead
of nodematch("type"). This will introduce two statistics in the model:

nodematch.type ?fund manager?=?fund manager?
nodematch.type ?broker?=?broker?

Combining with nodematch.lastjob you should be able to explain the
homophily effects.

Best,
Yun
